title: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders
summary: KZ Tandingan takes pride in seeing that many newcomers from all across the archipelago aren't afraid to sing in their mother tongue

items: The Filipino music scene is primarily centered in Metro Manila, where many successful artists begin their careers in local venues, often requiring aspiring musicians from provinces to travel long distances for auditions.

KZ Tandingan, a prominent singer-songwriter, rose to fame after winning X Factor Philippines in 2012, using her platform to advocate for music in various Philippine languages and to challenge traditional beauty standards in the industry.

Despite the challenges of accessibility in the music industry, Tandingan remains optimistic about the growing acceptance of diverse musical expressions in different languages, encouraging new artists to embrace their cultural roots.

The Filipino music scene has long largely operated in the metro, with many of today’s most successful local acts starting out as performers in dive bars around different cities close to the capital before their meteoric rise.
Major concerts are usually held in venues across Pasay and Quezon City, and the TV shows that are known to produce successful stars operate from Metro Manila, too.
And to get a shot at making it big, aspiring artists from provinces often have to travel long hours and spend thousands on plane rides just to audition for these music shows.

It’s a reality KZ Tandingan is all too familiar with. In 2012, the acclaimed singer-songwriter, who hails from Digos, Davao del Sur, packed her bags to audition for the first season of X Factor Philippines.

Just 20 years old then, Tandingan had joined the reality singing competition with a brave mission to help her family, and to prove that you didn’t need to conform to traditional beauty standards to become successful.

“Gusto ko pong sumali ng ‘X Factor’ hindi lang para tulungan ang pamilya ko, kung ‘di patunayan na ang industriya ng musika sa Philippines ay hindi lang para sa mga magaganda, sa mga makikinis ang balat, sa mga matatangkad, at sa mga biritero’t biritera,” she said during her audition.

(I want to join X Factor not just to help my family, but to prove that the music industry in the Philippines isn’t just for the beautiful, for those with clear skin, those who are tall, and those who can belt easily.)

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: Tandingan had confidently told the judges that she would sing her own version of “Somewhere Over The Rainbow,” and she had, right off the bat, proven that her soulful, raspy vocal tone would take her places far and wide. It was a goal she would see through at each round of the competition, until she would eventually emerge as X Factor Philippines’ first-ever winner.
And over a decade, countless chart-topping hits, and plenty of large-scale shows later, Tandingan has not once forgotten where she came from.

Tandingan had developed most of her career in Manila — having been signed to major record labels before going independent earlier this year. Despite being so far away from home all the time, she and her husband, fellow famed musician TJ Monterde, have made it a point to stand as staunch advocates of music sung in different languages across the Philippines.

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: “For a really, really long time, when music is recognized, artists who sing in their native tongue would always be boxed into that small category of regional music. I think a big factor is that we don’t expose the whole Philippines to all the songs sung in different languages,” Tandingan told Rappler in a mix of English and Filipino.
With the platform she’s built with her own craft, Tandingan then makes it a point to sing in Bisaya as much as she can.
Just take her latest Coke Studio track “Bugsay” for example. It’s sung entirely in Bisaya, and it was a creative choice Tandingan knew she had to make.

“‘Di ba, sabi nga nila, kunwari, nag-Bibisaya ako, tapos lumipat ako ng Manila, [nag-Fifilipino] na ako ngayon. If hindi ko ipapractice ‘yung Bisaya ko, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, makakalimutan mo ‘yun. And part ‘yun ng kultura ko as a Mindanaoan,” she told Rappler.

(They say that, for example, I speak Bisaya, then I moved to Manila and started speaking Filipino. If I don’t practice my Bisaya, if I don’t get to connect with my roots, you’ll forget it. And it’s part of my culture as a Mindanaoan.)
“Bugsay” is a Bisaya word for “oar.” It carries a strong message: to keep paddling, no matter how strong the current gets.

While the song strives to inspire those who listen to it, it bears a bigger aspiration for Tandingan: to make it known that there are songs by musicians from across the archipelago that aren’t just sung in Filipino or English. After all, some stories are better told in their original languages.

“If ‘Bugsay’ is able to [encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs], nagawa ko na ‘yung purpose ko as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — kasi Bisaya ako. Proud Bisdak talaga ako.”

(If “Bugsay” is able to encourage more Filipinos to listen to non-English and Filipino songs, I’ve fulfilled my purpose as an artist. That’s why it’s important for me to always champion my roots — because I’m Bisaya. I’m a proud Bisdak.)
The “Two Less Lonely People in the World” singer is still waiting for the day music auditions become more accessible to people from all over Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao.

“I know so many talented artists that weren’t given a chance to audition because of the fact that you have to pay for a plane ride to Manila. That’s already a luxury for so many talented musicians back home,” Tandingan said in a mix of Filipino and English.
There’s still a long way to go, but Tandingan remains hopeful.

blocks.caption: ‘Proud Bisdak’ KZ Tandingan wants Filipino music to transcend borders

blocks.text: “Masaya pa rin ako sa nangyayari sa atin ngayon kasi ang daming mga bagong salta na mga musician and they’re not afraid to sing in their own language. May mga kumakanta ng Ilocano, ng Bisaya, at Chavacano,” she mused.
(I’m still happy because there are so many newly minted musicians who aren’t afraid to sing in their own language. There are people who sing in Ilocano, in Bisaya, or in Chavacano.)

It’s always heartwarming for Tandingan to see Filipino musicians shine as they are. More and more Filipino artists are now unafraid to break out of the mold of what supposedly means to be successful, and are more than willing to gamble on the big possibility of virality that singing in more widely recognizable languages can give them.
Through it all, they do it all in the name of honoring the roots and the land they came from. – Rappler.com
